records.cool_rest_note: In autumn the pads shrivel and lie down as the plant withdraws water ahead of winter, becoming scraggly (though technically evergreen) through the cold months, then green up quickly again in spring (Missouri Botanical Garden).
records.name_note: The three admissible dedicated single-species pages lead with three different common names. NC State's Description prose calls the plant "Eastern prickly pear" and uses that name throughout the page, while its separate Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and stacks four entries (Devil's Tongue, Eastern Prickly Pear Cactus, Low Prickly Pear, Smooth Prickly Pear), so "Devil's Tongue" stands first in it. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder gives a single Common Name field value, "prickly-pear" (no "eastern," no "cactus"). RHS's page renders "spreading prickly pear" as its profile subtitle. common_name was set to "Eastern Prickly Pear," the name NC State's own dedicated-page prose leads with; the other two lead names are documented here rather than adopted. Distinct from Opuntia ficus-indica, which this catalog already carries as Prickly Pear.
records.toxicity_detail: Not a systemic-toxicity concern for pets: NC State's structured tags read "#non-toxic for cats," "#non-toxic for dogs," and (co-listed in the same tag block) "#non-toxic for horses." The real hazard is contact/handling, not ingestion-toxicity: NC State separately tags the plant "#contact dermatitis" and its structured Problems field lists "Contact Dermatitis" — NC State carries no separate human-scoped Poison rating block for this species, only this contact-hazard tag/field. NC State's handling guidance: "Use caution when handling this plant because the bristles can get into the skin and cause irritation. Wear protective gloves." Missouri Botanical Garden describes the same hazard in more clinical detail: "Pads have only scattered needle-like spines, but are covered with numerous tufts of bristles (glochids) which easily pierce human skin and can cause significant allergic skin reactions." On edibility, the two sources differ slightly in how far they extend it: NC State's Edibility field states "Fruit is used to make candies and jams. The pads can be eaten raw or cooked. Remove the bristles first." — an unrestricted (fruit-and-pad) edibility claim with an explicit bristle-removal precondition. Missouri Botanical Garden also calls the fruit edible ("used to make candies and jams") and separately notes that "Native Americans... roasted the pads as a vegetable," a historical/preparation-specific framing of pad use that does not repeat NC State's bristle-removal instruction.

RHS's Opuntia humifusa page is a thin profile. It carries no Position, Soil, pH or hardiness-rating fields; its Size section renders only Time to Maturity, with the value No preference, and no ultimate height or spread; and its Botanical Details block carries only Family (Cactaceae), Native to GB/Ireland (No), a genus-level Genus description, Name Status (Correct) and Plant Range (USA). It therefore could not corroborate or contradict soil, sun-hour or hardiness data for this species. RHS's Genus text is genus-level boilerplate and is not quoted here as species evidence.

RHS lists Opuntia mesacantha among this species' synonyms, while NC State treats Opuntia mesacantha as a distinct, frequently-confused sibling species with its own separate NC State page: NC State says O. mesacantha bears a few long pale spines up to 1 inch while O. humifusa has no spines on its pads, both species bearing glochids. That is an unresolved taxonomic disagreement between two admissible sources, noted here since it concerns species identity rather than a common-name split (which is covered in name_note). It also means NC State's spineless-pad statement sits against MoBot's "Pads have only scattered needle-like spines", the source disagreement disclosed in toxicity_detail.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the lead common name. NC State's dedicated Yucca filamentosa page leads its (alphabetized) Common Name(s) list with "Adam's Needle Yucca," UF/IFAS's dedicated FPS-615 page gives "Adam's needle" as its Common name(s) field (matching its own page heading), and Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder gives "Adam's needle" as its single Common Name field. RHS's dedicated page instead leads with the subtitle "needle palm" directly under its Yucca filamentosa H1; RHS's separate, secondary "Other common names" list includes "Adam's needle and thread" (not bare "Adam's needle") alongside Carolina silk grass, Our Lord's candle, spoonleaf yucca, and thready Adam's needle. Because three of the four dedicated-page sources lead with an Adam's Needle variant, "Adam's Needle" was used as common_name.
records.toxicity_detail: RHS's 'Potentially harmful' field (in its Botanical Details section) states: 'Skin allergen.  Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling' and separately 'Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten - for further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants' -- naming both cats and dogs specifically as at risk from ingestion, alongside a skin-contact/handling warning for people. NC State's dedicated page does not carry a dedicated 'Poison' block; instead its structured 'Problems' field tags this species 'Problem for Cats,' 'Problem for Dogs,' and 'Problem for Horses' -- an animal-scoped tag list, not a human-scoped severity rating, and it includes horses in addition to cats and dogs. The admissible sources disagree on human edibility: NC State's Edibility field states 'The edible flowers taste somewhat like bitter artichoke and can be used fresh in salads, cooked in soups or stews, or roasted,' while RHS flags the plant as a skin allergen and harmful to pets if eaten. There is also a mechanical hazard: NC State's whole-plant traits list 'Appendage: Spines,' and UF/IFAS advises 'Locate the plant 3 to 4 feet back from the edge of a walk or patio to prevent getting injured from the spine at the tip of the leaves.' No admissible source gave a poison-part list, symptom list, or severity rating beyond these items, so none is asserted here.
unknowns: is_houseplant is false: no admissible source frames this species as an indoor houseplant; every admissible source (NC State, UF/IFAS, RHS, MoBot) describes only outdoor/landscape cultivation, with USDA hardiness zones at NC State, UF/IFAS and MoBot and an RHS hardiness rating of H5 at RHS. The genus sibling already in this catalog, Yucca gigantea (Yucca Cane), is the Yucca framed as an indoor plant; no value in this record comes from that page. is_edible removed on audit: Fails the edibility-safety disclosure rule. The value's evidence is fine — NC State's Edibility field says verbatim 'The edible flowers taste somewhat like bitter artichoke and can be used fresh in salads, cooked in soups or stews, or roasted.', and 'Flower Value To Gardener: Edible' corroborates — and the flower-only scoping is correctly disclosed. But a consulted page names a harm that is absent from unknowns: the RHS details page (rhs.org.uk/plants/19164) carries a 'Potentially harmful' field reading 'Skin allergen. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling' and 'Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten'. The researcher read RHS (they quote its Max Height/Max Spread in unknowns) yet disclosed only the leaves' spine tips as a physical hazard, omitting the handling-allergen warning and the harmful-if-eaten note entirely. An is_edible true on a plant one consulted source flags as harmful if eaten by pets and requiring gloves to handle must carry that condition. NC State itself has zero hits for 'toxic' or 'poison', and UF/IFAS FP615 has zero hits for 'edib' or 'toxic', so RHS is the only hazard source and it was dropped. Null the field until the RHS 'Potentially harmful' condition is written into unknowns alongside the flower-only restriction.

records.name_note: Admissible dedicated single-species pages split on which common name leads. NC State's page carries a "Common Name(s)" list of six alphabetized names (Horseflyweed, Rattleweed, Shoofly, Wild Black Indigo, Wild Indigo, Yellow Wild Indigo), so "Horseflyweed" sorts first; its species Description opens "Yellow wild indigo is a native herbaceous perennial in the bean family (Fabaceae) native to eastern North America." RHS's and MoBot's dedicated pages each lead with the bare "wild indigo": RHS renders it as the common-name line beneath its "RHS Plant Profile" heading, with a separate "Other common names" list reading "clover broom, horse-flea weed, horsefly weed, indigo weed, North American wild indigo, rattle bush, rattle weed, shoo-fly, yellow indigo"; MoBot's structured field reads "Common Name: wild indigo". Bare "wild indigo" is, however, a genus-level name NC State also assigns to the siblings already in this catalog (Baptisia australis, Baptisia alba) and to the genus page itself, so the species-distinguishing "Yellow Wild Indigo" was used for common_name -- the name NC State's species prose leads with and the one MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics names alongside it ("commonly called wild indigo or yellow wild indigo"). "Wild Indigo" and "Horseflyweed" remain valid alternate names per NC State's list.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on which common name is primary. NC State Extension's Sedum ternatum page lists six common names under a stacked "Common Name(s)" heading in alphabetical order (Mountain Stonecrop, Stonecrop, Three-leaved Stonecrop, Whorled Stonecrop, Wild Stonecrop, Woodland Stonecrop); NC State's own Description prose calls the plant Mountain Stonecrop throughout. Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder carries a single rendered "Common Name" field whose value is "three-leaved stonecrop", and its Noteworthy Characteristics text says the species is "commonly called three-leaved stonecrop (also commonly called whorled stonecrop)" -- that lead name is the value used here. RHS's record for the same binomial lists "Iceland moss" under Other common names; that name belongs to an unrelated lichen and appears to be a database artefact (MoBot's own common-names list carries it too), so it was not used. Distinct from Sedum spectabile, which this catalog already carries as Showy Stonecrop.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Sedum ternatum page carries no Poisonous to Humans block (no severity rating, no poison-part list). Its warning appears in two places, both scoped to people. Description prose: "The sap can irritate the skin of some people and the leaves, eaten in quantity, can cause stomach upsets." Edibility field: "The stems and leaves, when very young and tender, may be eaten raw. Later, until they flower, they may be briefly cooked. When ingested in large quantities, can cause stomach upset." So the same source both permits limited human consumption of very young growth (raw when very young and tender; briefly cooked until flowering) and warns of skin irritation from sap and stomach upset in quantity. No animal is named anywhere on the page, so none of this supports a cats/dogs determination.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: the only toxicity language found on an admissible source (NC State Extension's 'the sap can irritate the skin of some people and the leaves, eaten in quantity, can cause stomach upsets') is scoped to people generally, naming no animal at all — it does not meet the cats/dogs-specific bar this field requires.

is_houseplant is false: every admissible source frames Sedum ternatum as a hardy outdoor woodland/garden groundcover (USDA zones 3a-9b per NC State), with no source framing it as a houseplant or discussing indoor/under-glass culture for this species specifically. The research record had left the field null; a landscape species with no houseplant framing lands false, as elsewhere in this catalog.

full_shade excluded from outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field for this species includes a 'Deep shade' tag, but that value is not corroborated by the structured sun fields of the other two admissible sources checked — RHS's Position field lists only 'Full sun', and Missouri Botanical Garden's structured Sun field reads 'Full sun to part shade' — so per the cross-source rule, deep/full shade is left out here though a gardener researching this species should know NC State lists it as shade-tolerant to that degree.

soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field for Sedum ternatum lists 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' and an open-ended 'Alkaline (>8.0)' tag, but RHS's pH field for the same species also lists alkaline soils as acceptable, so no defensible upper pH ceiling can be set from the closed top of NC State's Neutral band alone.

water_regime and the day-interval/dry-down fields left null: no admissible source frames watering for this in-ground perennial as a discrete regime. Missouri Botanical Garden's structured Water field reads 'Medium' (mid-scale, and per the scoring rule this alone cannot support keep_moist); NC State's Description prose adds only that the plant 'will tolerate full sun, seldom needs watering, and will grow in moist soils with good drainage'. Neither rises to a stated watering regimen matching one of the four enum options.

chill_damage_f, day/night temperature fields, humidity fields, light_fc fields, direct_sun_hours_max, and all fertilize_* fields left null: no admissible source states numeric values, onset-damage temperatures, footcandle levels, species-specific sun-hour prose, or fertilizing guidance for Sedum ternatum. (NC State's Light field does carry generic hour ranges, e.g. '6 or more hours' for its Full sun category, but per instructions that is the site-wide light-category legend, not species-specific prose, so it was not used for direct_sun_hours_max.)

RHS's structured Position field for this species reads 'Full sun'. Its Cultivation paragraph is separate and reads in full 'Grow in a sheltered position in moderately fertile, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun. See hardy cacti and succulent cultivation for further advice' -- generic hardy-succulent guidance that closes by pointing at a genus-level advice page, so it was not leaned on; RHS's own species description ('A compact, evergreen succulent, to around 15cm high, with a creeping habit, branching stems and flat, broadly oval to rounded, fleshy green leaves arranged in whorls of 3 around the stems.') is unmistakably species-level. The sibling-page boilerplate check the research record claimed against Sedum acre could not be reproduced at landing (RHS's sibling page did not serve content), so that assurance is unverified. RHS's 'Full sun' Position framing sits in some tension with the North American sources' shade-tolerant woodland framing; only the shade values its structured field excludes were dropped from outdoor_sun_exposure.
